items.q: Fats had this tune, but he didn’t have it completed, and he asked me to work on it with him

ctx.x: Basie’s style at that time was pretty much like most of the Harlem pianists, Fats Waller and, oh, was it J. P. Johnson?

items.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I know that we played in what we called a spaghetti joint in Brooklyn

ctx.x: Well, one thing that I can remember [laughs]. You know, he was a very, very sort of brusque but not abrasive, not abrasive character. Sort of brusque and, you know, but a tough papa kind of thing, you know, but very warm and lovable once you got to know him. Having played the C melody saxophone and then gotten to the alto, I wasn’t used to playing in the concert keys . . . I mean, in the other keys, other than the concert key, the same key in which he was playing. You know, so when I would be playing in C on the…
Do you remember some of the places you worked with Willy “The Lion”?

Not by name at the moment. One thing stands out in my mind. I know that we played in what we called a spaghetti joint in Brooklyn, and what we think were some mobsters came in one night and kind of shot up the place. I think I got out of there, but Willy found or sought refuge in the gents’ room and stayed there until, you know, the thing was over. We used to kid him about it, you know. But everybody was dodging and trying to get out of their way.

items.title: 66095_Benny Carter oral history interview
items.q: And it was a very valuable musical experience for me, playing with him. ... And that's the first time that you worked regularly with Fats Waller on a project? Yes, yes.

ctx.x: Did you -- was Fats active -- Fat Warner, active around that time? He must have been, I suppose.
Yes, Fats was active. I think at that time, he was playing the organ at the Lincoln Theatre, I think
was the name of it on 135th Street. He was very active indeed. And of course ...
